newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian interest rates head downward.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian interest rates head downward.

text.p: Low demand for lending and high liquidity are some of the factors pushing interest rates lower in Nigeria just weeks after an official ceiling on rates was lifted, bankers said on Friday.
"The trend is downward and it is obvious that both lending and deposits rates are now well below the official cap," said a spokesman for the Money Market Association of Nigeria (MMAN).
Lending rates have fallen to between 16 and 18 percent this week from the 21 percent at which it was pegged until early October.
"We expect lending rates to fall even further because the system is liquid and the low level of economic activity means there are not many borrowers around," the MMAN spokesman said.
Deposit rates in some banks are as low as 10 percent from around 16 percent previously.
"Because of the current hardship in the country not too many people are saving," one treasury manager said.

He said much of the new money in the system were deposits by the Petroleum Trust Fund (PTF), set up by the government last year to utilise for the common good money realised from a fourfold increase in pump prices in October 1994.
PTF is headed by former military ruler retired Major-General Muhammed Buhari and has been spending heavily on road rehabilitation and supply of drugs to cash-strapped public hospitals.
Some bankers said the PTF deposits were the main factor in pushing interest rates down.
Between September and October it pumped in two tranches of six billion naira each into selected banks for specific periods at interest rates bankers said were largely dictated by the fund.
Other bankers said the lower trend in bank rates was due to low demand for funds by manufacturers.
"Industries are not borrowing because their warehouses are full as a result of low consumer demand," one said.
"No one is borrowing and in an attempt by banks to go on lending because that is what banking is all about they have had to lower rates at least to prime customers," he added.
Bankers have generally hailed the freeing of interest rates which Nigeria's military government has held up as part of its gradual deregulation of sub-Saharan Africa's biggest economy.

They said this could contribute to renewed economic activity in a country where fiscal discipline and pragmatic policies have succeeded in stabilising the economy but not yet brought the growth required to stimulate demand.
